justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a broadly stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 295.5 is anchored primarily to recent price levels and momentum, assuming no major overnight or early-session catalysts. Markets tend to exhibit mean-reversion over very short windows absent fresh news, so the one-day figure stays close to the prevailing level. The slight upward progression from 295.5 to 296.0 at one week and 297.0 at one month reflects a small positive drift assumption consistent with the long-run historical tendency of equity markets to grind higher when macroeconomic conditions are not acutely deteriorating. I did not embed a strong directional view; rather, the drift is conservative and reflects baseline expectations rather than a specific macro call.

The confidence interval widths expand as expected across horizons, reflecting how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 12 points, consistent with typical daily realized volatility in a large-cap index or ETF context. By one week, the interval widens to 24 points, roughly capturing the square-root-of-time scaling one would expect if daily moves are roughly independent. At one month, the interval stretches to 48 points, acknowledging that over four or five weeks, cumulative shocks — earnings surprises, Federal Reserve communications, geopolitical developments, or shifts in credit conditions — can meaningfully move prices away from current levels. Implied volatility conditions at the time of the forecast also informed these widths, with options markets pricing in moderate but not extreme uncertainty.

There are several risks that could push realized outcomes outside these intervals entirely. On the downside, an unexpected tightening shock — such as a hotter-than-expected inflation print prompting hawkish Fed repricing — could trigger a sharp selloff well below the lower bound, particularly over the one-week and one-month horizons. A credit event, liquidity squeeze, or geopolitical escalation could similarly produce tail moves. On the upside, a surprisingly dovish policy signal, strong economic data, or a breakthrough in a major geopolitical standoff could fuel a rally beyond the upper bound. These fat-tail events are by definition underrepresented in symmetric confidence intervals, so the true distribution of outcomes has heavier tails than a normal approximation would suggest.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging model limitations. My estimates implicitly assume continuity in market structure and liquidity conditions. Circuit breakers, trading halts, or extreme illiquidity episodes — rare but non-negligible — could make intraday or weekly outcomes discontinuous in ways that render these intervals misleading.
